subject: Difference between predictor from inla.posterior.sample and computed from the latent field

messages.author: fb1667ba74f25458
messages.subject: Difference between predictor from inla.posterior.sample and computed from the latent field
parts:
Hi,
I am trying to do prediction with samples from a large model. The model is expensive to fit, so getting predictions via refitting the model is not an option. The approach I take is that I use inla.posterior.sample to generate samples and plugin the samples coefficients to compute the linear predictor myself. As a sanity check, I looked if I can recover the "Predictor:XXXX" values in the samples. I am however unable to do this exactly, in particular the "Predictor:XXXX" values tend to be systematically slightly lower than what I compute myself. A short example using the binomial likelihood:
-----

library(INLA)
library(tidyverse)

logistic <- function(x) { 1 / (1 + exp(-x))}

n <- 10
data.test <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n,0,1)) %>% mutate(y = rbinom(n,size = 3, logistic(x * 1 + 5)))


ff <- inla(y ~ 1 + x , data = data.test, control.compute = list(config = TRUE), family = "binomial",Ntrials = 3)

st <- inla.posterior.sample(n= 1, ff)

expected_predictor <- st[[1]]$latent["(Intercept)",] + data.test$x * st[[1]]$latent["x",] 

predictor_inla <- st[[1]]$latent[1:n]

data.frame(expected_predictor,predictor_inla) %>% mutate(difference = expected_predictor - predictor_inla)

st[[1]]$latent


-------
The difference is quite big and is systematic. I also tested with normal and Poison likelihoods, where there is a difference, but much smaller and not ostensibly biased in one direction.

Do you have any ideas why this is the case? Is this expected behavior for some reason?

Thanks for any hints
Martin

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Difference between predictor from inla.posterior.sample and computed from the latent field
parts:
Hi,

attached is a slight modified example. there are two issues.

1. the simulated example submitted origianlly was kind of extreme.
N(0,1)'s might go from [-3, 3] and as a covariate in a logisistic
regression this is kind of extreme when the coefficient is 1 and the
intercept 5.

I added a more reasonable example, which is much better in terms of the
results, but the main problem is still there.


2. the simulations only do the gaussian case, but with a corrected
mean. if you plot the marginals of the linear predictor, like

plot(inla.smarginal(ff$marginals.linear.predictor[[1]])))

then you see its skewed. The mean computed internally in inla() take
this into account, but the simulations does not as it assumes
gaussianity.

3. however, the skewness *IS* reported in the configurations, like

> ff$misc$configs$config[[1]]$skewness
[1] 0.3932938692 0.2259272033 0.2885080649 0.2648410231 0.2876844
368
[6] 0.2717283250 0.4015066353 0.4023276288 0.2662903562 0.2656046
594
[11] 0.2747033050 -0.1824522288

but it is currently not used. it is possible to adjust the simulations
for this (using the same copula, but adjusting each one for the
skewness)

4. The extention is a little bit of work, but straight forward.

5. I'm happy to work with anyone who wants to push this extention
forward.

Best
H
